a: The hope of life is the beginning and end of our faith. Righteousness is the beginning and end of judgment. Love, shown in gladness and joy, is the testimony of the works of righteousness.
p: Lake calls the passage "confused." C, Sinaiticus and the Latin each have a different text.

readings.w: Lake's text, from Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, written in AD 1056), from Lake's footnote
readings.orig: ζωῆς ἐλπίς, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος πίστεως ἡμῶν· καὶ δικαιοσύνη, κρίσεως ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος· ἀγάπη εὐφροσύνης καὶ ἀγαλλιάσεως ἔργων δικαιοσύνης μαρτυρία
readings.en: the hope of life, beginning and end of our faith; and righteousness, beginning and end of judgment; love of gladness and joy, testimony of works of righteousness
readings.plain: The hope of life is the beginning and end of our faith. Righteousness is the beginning and end of judgment. Love, shown in gladness and joy, is the testimony of the works of righteousness.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Lake's footnote
readings.orig: ζωή, πίστις, ἐλπίς, ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος ἡμῶν, καὶ δικαιοσύνη κρίσεως ἀρχή, καὶ τέλος ἀγάπη, εὐφροσύνη, καὶ ἀγαλλιάσεως ἔργων ἐν δικαιοσύναις μαρτυρία
readings.en: life, faith, hope, our beginning and end; and righteousness, beginning of judgment; and end, love, gladness, and testimony of joy of works in righteous deeds
readings.plain: Life, faith and hope are our beginning and end. Righteousness is the beginning of judgment, and the end is love. Gladness is the testimony of joy in works done in righteousness.

why: Lake prints the text of C, which "gives the best sense, though it is doubtful if it is more than the correction of an early corruption." Sinaiticus's list does not make three teachings, and the Latin stops short. The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The English of the second reading is only one way to read a jumbled Greek.

p: Sinaiticus has "to God," as the Greek Psalm 51 does.

p: The copies say "clothes." A corrector of Sinaiticus wrote "healing," as Greek Isaiah 58:8 has.

p: Sinaiticus has "newcomers"; C and the Latin have "proselytes," converts to the Jewish law.

p: Sinaiticus asks what they are to do; C and G ask what they will do.

why: Lake prints Sinaiticus's subjunctive, a question about what the rite requires. C and G have the future. The two forms differ by one letter in Greek, and the question in 7:6 ("what does he command?") fits the subjunctive.

t: Words only in G and the Latin
p: Sinaiticus and C leave out "And again the Spirit of the Lord prophesies."

why: Lake prints the words, though Codex Sinaiticus and C lack them. Without them the next quotation runs straight on from "the Lord your God says." The phrase fits the writer's habit of "and again ... says" between quotations, and a copyist's eye could have skipped from one "and again" to the next.

a: whether he has given the covenant that he swore to the fathers he would give to the people.
p: C, G and the Latin add "let us seek," and G rewrites the sentence.

readings.w: Lake's text: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Lake's footnote
readings.orig: ἀλλὰ ἴδωμεν, εἰ ἡ διαθήκη, ἣν ὤμοσεν τοῖς πατράσιν δοῦναι τῷ λαῷ, εἰ δέδωκεν.
readings.en: but let us see whether the covenant which he swore to the fathers to give to the people, whether he has given it
readings.plain: whether he has given the covenant that he swore to the fathers he would give to the people.

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, written in AD 1056), from Lake's footnote; the eight later Greek manuscripts that run Polycarp to the Philippians 9 into Barnabas 5 (their common ancestor, G), from Lake's footnote; the Latin version (L, one manuscript, ending at 17:2), from Lake's footnote, which also changes the start of the sentence (Lake: "the grammar of the sentence is emended by G"); the Latin version (L, one manuscript, ending at 17:2), from Lake's footnote
readings.en: ... whether he has given it, let us seek
readings.plain: about the covenant that he swore to the fathers he would give to the people: let us seek whether he has given it.

why: Lake prints Sinaiticus, whose sentence repeats "whether" and is rough. The added "let us seek" in C, G and the Latin smooths it, and G smooths it further. The sense is the same.

a: And he threw the tablets out of his hands
p: G and the Latin write "the tablets"; Sinaiticus and C leave the object unstated.

readings.w: Lake's text: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Lake's footnote; Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, written in AD 1056), from Lake's footnote
readings.en: and he threw [them] out of his hands
readings.plain: And he threw the tablets out of his hands

readings.w: the eight later Greek manuscripts that run Polycarp to the Philippians 9 into Barnabas 5 (their common ancestor, G), from Lake's footnote; the Latin version (L, one manuscript, ending at 17:2), from Lake's footnote; the Latin version (L, one manuscript, ending at 17:2), from Lake's footnote
readings.orig: καὶ ἔρριψεν ἐκ τῶν χειρῶν τὰς πλάκας
readings.en: and he threw out of his hands the tablets
readings.plain: And he threw the tablets out of his hands

why: Lake prints the shorter text, where "threw" has no object in Greek. English needs one, and the clause before speaks of idols, so the Plain English Translation supplies "the tablets" from 4:8 and the end of this verse. The English is the same for both readings; G and the Latin write out what Sinaiticus and C leave understood.

a: the good news of grace to the lowly
p: G has "grace to the lowly," the Latin "the lowly," Sinaiticus "the poor," as Greek Isaiah 61:1 and Luke 4:18 have.

readings.w: Lake's text: the eight later Greek manuscripts that run Polycarp to the Philippians 9 into Barnabas 5 (their common ancestor, G), from Lake's footnote

readings.plain: the good news of grace to the lowly

readings.en: to the lowly
readings.plain: the good news to the lowly

readings.en: to tell good news to the poor
readings.plain: the good news to the poor

why: Lake prints G. Sinaiticus agrees with the Greek Isaiah, which copyists knew well. The difference between the poor and the lowly is small in the Bible's language (compare Isaiah 61:1 in the Hebrew, where the site has "the humble").

a: in my eagerness, I have not left out anything that has to do with salvation
p: Some copies have only "that I have not left anything out."

readings.en: by my desire not to have left out anything of the things that belong to salvation

readings.w: the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ*), from Lake's footnote
readings.en: not to have left out anything

why: Lake prints the longer text. "In my eagerness" and "that has to do with salvation" stand only in it; the shorter text says the same in fewer words.

p: C and G have "two-tongued," the Didache's word. G also adds the Didache's next line.

readings.w: Lake's text: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Lake's footnote
readings.en: nor talkative

readings.w: Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, written in AD 1056), from Lake's footnote
readings.en: nor two-tongued

readings.w: the eight later Greek manuscripts that run Polycarp to the Philippians 9 into Barnabas 5 (their common ancestor, G), from Lake's footnote, which adds a line Lake traces to the Apostolic Constitutions
readings.orig: οὐδὲ δίγλωσσος· παγὶς γὰρ θανάτου ἐστὶν ἡ διγλωσσία
readings.en: nor two-tongued; for double-tonguedness is a snare of death
readings.plain: or two-tongued, for a double tongue is a death trap

why: Lake prints Sinaiticus. C and G agree with Didache 2:4, and G copies the Didache's whole line, which Lake says came in from the Apostolic Constitutions (a later church order that took over the Didache). A copyist was more likely to bring Barnabas into line with the familiar text than to change "two-tongued" to a rarer word. The English of the third reading is the site's Didache 2:4.

p: G and the Latin read "of them," the commandments; Sinaiticus and C read "of yourselves."

readings.w: Lake's text: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), from Lake's footnote; Codex Constantinopolitanus (C, written in AD 1056), from Lake's footnote

readings.w: the eight later Greek manuscripts that run Polycarp to the Philippians 9 into Barnabas 5 (their common ancestor, G), from Lake's footnote; the Latin version (L, one manuscript, ending at 17:2), from Lake's footnote
readings.en: do not fall short in any of them

why: Lake prints Codex Sinaiticus and C. His own English translation, though, reads "fail not in any of them," which follows the other reading. The phrase also stood in 21:2 ("Do not fail them").
